questions.question: Why does Haskell reject `(+) == (*)`?
options: + and * have different types
Functions have no Eq instance, because there is no general way to decide whether two functions compute the same results
== only works on numbers
+ and * are not defined for the same types
questions.explanation: Both (+) and (*) have type Num a => a -> a -> a — the types match. The rejection is that function types are simply not members of Eq at all: deciding function equality in general is not computable, so no instance is (or could be) provided.
optionFeedback: Both are Num a => a -> a -> a; the types line up exactly, so a type mismatch is not the issue.
Correct — there is no Eq instance for function types at all, for any two functions, regardless of what they compute.
== is overloaded across many non-numeric types too — Bool, Char, String, custom types — so this is not a numbers-only restriction.
Num a => a -> a -> a is shared by both; the rejection has nothing to do with whether their types line up.

questions.question: Given `data Result = Pass | Fail deriving (Ord)`, why is `Pass < Fail` True?
options: Pass is alphabetically before Fail
A derived Ord ranks constructors by their declaration order, and Pass is declared first
Ord always ranks the first-listed value as larger
It is arbitrary and could change between runs
questions.explanation: A derived Ord instance ranks constructors purely by the order they appear in the data declaration — first declared is smallest. Pass appears before Fail, so Pass < Fail.
optionFeedback: Alphabetically, F comes before P — that is not the rule in force here, or Fail would be smaller.
Correct — deriving Ord ranks constructors by declaration order; Pass was written first, so it compares as smaller.
The opposite is true: the first-declared constructor ranks smallest, not largest.
It is fixed by the source file's declaration order and is identical on every run — nothing about it is arbitrary.

questions.question: Why does `compare (1, "a") (2, "a")` return LT without ever comparing the strings?
options: Tuples only ever compare their first component
Tuple comparison inspects components left to right and stops as soon as one pair disagrees; the first components (1 and 2) already disagree
"a" cannot be compared to itself
GHC evaluates tuples right to left
questions.explanation: Tuple Ord compares component by component from the left, moving to the next component only when the current ones are equal. Since 1 and 2 already differ, the result is settled immediately and the second components are never examined.
optionFeedback: The earlier example, compare (1, "b") (1, "a"), shows the second component deciding the result when the first components tie — so later components do matter.
Correct — comparison proceeds left to right and short-circuits at the first disagreement, exactly as list comparison does.
Comparing a value to an equal copy of itself is perfectly well defined and would report EQ; that is not why it is skipped here.
Tuple fields are logically compared left to right, matching how they are written and read, not right to left.

questions.question: For the Student example, why does read (show k) :: Student round-trip back to a value equal to k?
options: Because Student derives Eq, which automatically fixes any mismatch between show and read
Because a derived Show and a derived Read for the same type are genuine inverses — the exact text a derived Show produces is exactly the text a derived Read for that type can parse back
Because Student has only two fields, and round-tripping only works for small records
It is a coincidence specific to this one value of Student
questions.explanation: Show and Read are deliberately designed as a matched pair when both are derived: show's textual format is precisely what read for that type expects to parse. Eq only lets you check the round trip afterwards — it does not cause the round trip to succeed.
optionFeedback: Eq only supplies == so the round trip can be checked after the fact; it plays no role in making show's output parseable by read in the first place.
Correct — deriving both gives you an inverse pair by construction, which is exactly why read (show k) reproduces k.
Nothing about the round trip depends on field count; the same guarantee holds for a record with many more fields.
The same round trip holds for any value of any type that derives both Show and Read — it is a general property of the derived instances, not a one-off.

questions.question: print (read "42") on its own is rejected as an ambiguous type variable, but read "42" + (1 :: Integer) is not. Why?
options: read always needs an annotation, with no exceptions

In the second expression, + forces read's result to be the same type as 1 :: Integer, so the context already pins down which Read instance to use; the first expression has nothing else that fixes the type
print cannot accept the result of read under any circumstances
"42" is only valid input for read when it appears next to +
questions.explanation: read's ambiguity comes from having no way to tell, from the text alone, which type was intended. Whenever the surrounding expression already pins that type down — here, addition with an Integer — no separate annotation is needed; otherwise, one must be added by hand.
optionFeedback: The + example is the counterexample: read needs an annotation only when nothing else in the expression already determines the target type.
Correct — the addition with (1 :: Integer) supplies exactly the missing type information that print (read "42") lacks on its own.
print works perfectly well on the result of read once that result's type is determined some other way, as the + example shows.
The text "42" is unrelated to why annotation is or isn't needed; the deciding factor is whether the surrounding expression fixes the result type.

questions.question: Why does `average xs = sum xs / length xs` fail to compile for `average :: [Double] -> Double`?
options: sum xs has type [Double], not Double
length xs always has type Int, but / requires both operands to share one Fractional type, and Int is not Fractional
/ cannot appear inside a function body
average needs a type class constraint on its own signature
questions.explanation: sum xs is a Double, matching the signature — the mismatch is entirely on the other side of /. length always returns Int, and / demands both arguments be the same Fractional type, which Int never is.
optionFeedback: sum :: Num a => [a] -> a applied to a [Double] correctly gives a Double; that side of the division is fine.
Correct — length xs :: Int cannot be given directly to /, which needs a Fractional argument; fromIntegral bridges the gap.
/ is an ordinary function and may appear anywhere an expression is expected, including inside average's body.
average's signature, [Double] -> Double, is already fully concrete; no class constraint is needed on it at all — the problem is internal to the body.

questions.question: What does round 2.5 evaluate to in Haskell, and why?
options: 3, because round always rounds halfway values up
2, because round breaks exact ties by rounding to the nearest even integer
2, because round always rounds down
It is an error, because 2.5 is ambiguous
questions.explanation: Haskell's round uses round-half-to-even: an exact tie rounds to whichever neighbouring integer is even. 2.5 is exactly halfway between 2 and 3, and 2 is even, so it rounds to 2.
optionFeedback: This is the 'round half up' rule used by some other languages and tools, but it is not what Haskell's round does for an exact tie.
Correct — round-half-to-even sends the exact tie 2.5 to 2, the nearest even integer, not to 3.
round does not always round down — round 2.7 gives 3, rounding up, as the program above shows; only exact ties use the even rule.
2.5 :: Double is a perfectly well-defined value; round has a fixed, documented rule for it and does not error.
